April 17, 2025 - Testimony in support of LD 1353:
"An Act Regarding Required Landings in the Menhaden Fishery"
Good afternoon Senator Tepler, Representative Hepler, and members of the Joint Standing
Committee on Marine Resources. Thank you for the opportunity to testiw today. My name is
Representative Billy Bob Faulkingham, and I serve as the House Republican Leader. I represent House District 12, which includes Franklin, Gouldsboro, Hancock, Sorrento, Sullivan, Winter Harbor, and
Steuben.
l'm here today to testify in support of LD 1353 -- "An Act Regarding Required Landings in the Menhaden Fishery." This bill offers a fair and narrowly tailored pathway for experienced menhaden
fishermen to maintain access to the fishery in 2026, even if they did not hold a license in the immediate prior year.
As it stands, current law restricts license eligibility to individuals who held one the previous year. While intended to help manage the fishery, this one-size-fits-all approach can unfairly disqualify fishermen who were active in the fishery in recent years but missed a season due to circumstances
beyond their control, such as illness, boat repairs, or shifting bait demand.
LD 1353 fixes this by allowing eligibility in 2026 for fishermen who:
~ Landed at least 20,000 lbs. of menhaden in any one of the years between 2019-2022; and
~ held a commercial menhaden license in at least two of those years.
This is a targeted exception that rewards legitimate participation without opening the door to new
entrants or undermining our marine conservation goals.
The Atlantic menhaden is both ecologically critical, as forage for striped bass, bluefish, and marine mammals, and economically vital as a bait source for Maine's lobster fishery, reducing our reliance on imported bait. The Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission (ASMFC) manages the species under a quota system, and Maine has been a consistent and compliant partner in that effort.
Unfortunately, the current carryover rule threatens to shut out the very fishermen who helped build this fishery, individuals who have demonstrated sustained, responsible activity but missed one
qualifying year.

LD 1353 maintains DMR's authority, keeps quota and reporting safeguards intact, and creates a limited exception based on performance, not preference. It supports working fishermen, protects the
critical bait supply for our lobster industry, and ensures this fishery remains local and sustainable.
For coastal communities like those I represent, this is about more than numbers. It's about protecting livelihoods, honoring hard work, and keeping Maine's working waterfront healthy and strong. l respectfully urge the Committee to vote Ought to Pass on LD 1353. Thank you for your time and your commitment to Maine's fisheries.
_
Respectfully,

190604:
TESTIMONY OF
Deirdre Gilbert
Department of Marine Resources
The Department of Marine Resources (DMR) is testifying
In Opposition to
LD 1353 An Act Regarding Required Landings in the Menhaden Fishery Before the Committee on Marine Resources
Sponsored by Representative Faulkingham Date of Hearing: April 17, 2025
Senator Tepler, Representative Hepler, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Marine
Resources, my name is Deirdre Gilbert, Director of State Marine Policy for DMR and I am testifying on
behalf of the Department in opposition to LD 1353.
Eligibility criteria for commercial menhaden licenses were first established ahead of the 2023 licensing year. ln order to be eligible for a 2023 license, harvesters needed to meet both a licensing standard (having been licensed for 2 years in 2019, 2020, and 2021) as well as a landings criteria (at least 25,000 lbs of landings in any of those years). The Department bill was amended in committee to expand participation by allowing individuals to meet the landings criteria in the 2022 fishing season. In the subsequent session, participation was expanded further, to allow having held a 2022 license to qualify as one of the two licensing years.
LD 1353 would further expand participation, by lowering the landings criteria from 25,000 to 20,000 lbs, as well as allowing license holders to submit qualifying landings from as far back as 2019 until January 1, 2026.
DMR can analyze the effect of lowering the landings criteria from 25,000 to 20,000 lbs with regard to
landings that have previously been submitted, and there are at least 20 more individuals who would become eligible for a license in 2026. However, the provision of the bill that allows a license holder to
submit landings from 2019, 2020, 2021 or 2022 until January 1, 2026 is far more difficult to assess and much more concerning.
While some menhaden is sold through dealers, many sales are also through the harvester to the end
user, so there is no corresponding dealer record to verify the validity of a harvester report. The opportunity to report landings from over 5 years ago in order to qualify for a license would reward
those individuals who are willing to falsify those reports and the Department would have nothing to
dispute any records received.
As the Department has explained in previous legislation, DMR does not think it is advisable to keep
altering the eligibility criteria for commercial menhaden licenses to continue to allow new subsets of
prior license holders in. Because of the opportunity to achieve the landings requirement of 25,000 lbs
in 2022, anyone who wanted this license has already had the opportunity to meet that very modest threshold. A broad opportunity to submit reports from seasons going back over 5 years could also

mean that Maine's quota is shown to have been exceeded, which could damage our standing with other states. For these reasons, we urge you to vote ought not to pass on LD 1353.
Thank you for your consideration and I wouid be happy to answer any questions you may have.
10044845:
Eric Staples Swan's Island LD 1353
I am writing today in favor of LD 1353. As a fourth generation lobsterman and a long time member of the Swan's Island fisherman's coop I am happy to see that this bill even exists. As a child, growing up in the 80's and early 90's, I have seen so many commercial fishing opportunities disappear. A "lobster boat" used to have many uses. Scolloping and sea urchin tending are the big ones that come to mind with stories of mackerel and pogie fishing attached to those memories. The return of the menhaden to the area a few short years ago was like a gift from God. In a small town such as Swan's Island it was especially exciting. The opportunity to make a living in more than one fishery was something new for anyone my age or younger. I know many people, including myself, that saw the fish and the opportunity and started to invest in the fishery. The abundance of fish was too hard to deny and for the willing, it was a way to save money on bait and possibly make a little profit with the every looming threat of the doom of the lobster industry being ever present. I MUST add that I did not and do not meet the requirements of this bill to receive a license if passed. But I do know many who invested time and money and most of all effort, who should, and deserve to retain their license. Government overreach and regulations based on zero common sense seem to be the theme of todays America. The fish are here, they may move on as they have in the past, let these men and women work before it's too late. Sooner the better!
10045080:
Jason Joyce Swan's Island LD 1353
Dear Committee Members,
Swan's Island is an unbridged island fishing community located 5 miles south of Mount Desert Island. My name is Jason Joyce and I am a lobsterman and Town Selectman writing on behalf of our fishing community and our need for at least 1 commercial license to catch the menhaden in our waters. Bait access and rising prices are two of the obstacles our lobstermen struggle with, but unlike most midcoast communities we do not have any commercially licensed menhaden fishermen in town. Swan's Island had 3 fishermen who invested in a boat, gear and nets and landed over 25k lbs in the last year of open licenses but they didn't have 2 years of landings in the following year and were unable to qualify for licenses. The boat and Gear have remained dormant, but the year they fished they supplied locally caught menhaden to our fisherman's co-op. I ask on behalf of my town for a mechanism that will enable our 3 fishermen to qualify to commercially land menhaden which in turn benefits the rest of our fishing community with access to locally caught and affordable fresh bait. Please move this bill forward with an "ought to pass" that helps our fishermen.
Thank you
10044885:
Matt Williams Swans island LD 1353
Im a Swans Island resident and bought a boat and gear in 2021 to fish the 2022 menhaden season,a total investment of $85k. I previously testified in person when the license retraction bill was discussed. Since the retraction the distribution of activity used licenses are concentrated from zone c down. We are an unabridged island all bait comes by ferry, herring quota was cut causing the forecasted price to go up. Hard bait is mostly a canadian product eligible for tariffs. With out a licensed fisherman in the conservation zone we pay higher than market value for menhaden. Something must be done to allow the fisherman that made large investments to participate in a fishery, participate again. The zone a and b lobsterman need the cheap bait
10057456:
Warren Graybill Harpswell LD 1353
To Whom it may concern,
My name is Warren Graybill Jr and I am a fisherman from Harpswell. I held a commercial menhaden license in 2020. I did not fish in 2021 so did not purchase a license due to it being an open fishery and not fishing. I was going to go back fishing in 2022, but, the fishery capped licenses based on 2 out of 3 years being 2019, 2020 and 2021. I decided not to rig my boat back up, buy a license and go fishing, knowing that I would not have been able to purchase a 2023 license or and years after. Then in 2023 a bill was introduced that allowed 2022 to then be used as a 2 years out of 4 eligibility. I had well over the required landings in one year, but not the 2 out of 3 licenses. If this bill was altered to allow the guys like me that only missed 2022 from qualifying for a license, it wouldn't have that big of an impact on the license number. Please consider amending this license to be 1 out of those 4 years, so that those of us that missed 2022 can go back fishing.
Thank you for your time and consideration. Warren Graybill Jr Harpswell
